paras: The lynching of L. M. Bell was the hanging of a planter, called Colonel Bell, by a mob near Hamburg, Arkansas, close to the Louisiana line, on the night of December 27, 1881. Bell was accused of beating his wife so badly that she died at Christmas, and neighbors took him from his home and hanged him to a tree. Wire reports carried the story across the country, and several papers presented the lynching as deserved.

Bell was described as "a prominent planter" living near Hamburg, near the line between Arkansas and Louisiana, and one digest version placed his home in Ashley County. A report from Pine Bluff said he "habitually abused his wife, an estimable woman," and that she died on Christmas "a victim of his brutality." A dispatch from Shreveport, Louisiana, instead said that she died on Monday, December 26, and was buried by friends.

According to the Shreveport dispatch, the wife's death so excited the neighborhood that a mob was organized on Tuesday night. The mob took Bell from his home and hanged him to a tree, where his body was found hanging the next morning. Another version said "a mob of indignant citizens" dragged him from his residence and hanged him to "an adjacent tree," and the Staunton Vindicator said "villagers and neighboring farmers" did it on the night of the funeral. No account names any member of the mob or gives its size.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no local Arkansas paper's account was found.

The first report found was a Pine Bluff special in the Chicago Tribune on December 29, which presented the hanging as a report that had "just reached" the town and printed the name as "Boll." The fuller Shreveport dispatch appeared the next day in papers from Los Angeles and Cheyenne to the Alexandria Gazette, and a short Hamburg dispatch in the Portland Daily Press called him "Col. J. M. Bell." Through January 1882 shortened versions kept running in weekly news digests such as the Richmond (Mo.) Democrat, the St. Landry Democrat, the Elk County Advocate and the Abbeville Press and Banner.

Headlines took the accusation as fact and the lynching as justified, calling Bell a "Brutal Husband" and a "Wife-Beater" and his death "A Merited Fate." Wisconsin papers ran the story under the pun "Bell-Hangers." The Staunton Vindicator called it "the best use that lynch law has been put to for a long time" and quoted a maxim that a man who strikes a woman is a coward. Most texts still attributed the beating to report, writing that Bell "is said to have" abused his wife or that "it is alleged" he did, and no version mentions race.

The versions differ on details: the Pine Bluff report put Bell's home about twenty-eight miles from Hamburg, while the Hamburg dispatch put the hanging twenty miles south of the town. The wife's death is dated to Christmas in the Pine Bluff and Hamburg reports and to Monday, December 26, in the Shreveport dispatch. Most reports place the lynching on Tuesday night, December 27, but the Hamburg dispatch dated December 29 says it happened "yesterday."

bases: Separate Pine Bluff, Shreveport and Hamburg dispatches report that a mob took Bell from his home and hanged him to a tree, accusing him of beating his wife to death (A1, A4, A5).

Bell was hanged without any legal process by a 'mob' organized in the neighborhood, described as 'villagers and neighboring farmers' (A3, A5, A15), in punishment for his alleged fatal beating of his wife (A1, A4).

Three separately datelined reports, from Pine Bluff (A1), Shreveport (A5) and Hamburg (A4), agree that a mob hanged Bell for causing his wife's death, though they differ on his initials, the dates and the distance from Hamburg.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff report
accounts.gist: A report reaching Pine Bluff on Dec. 28 said Col. L. M. Boll, living on the Arkansas-Louisiana line about 28 miles from Hamburg, had been hung by a mob after his wife died on Christmas, allegedly from his habitual abuse.

accounts.label: Shreveport dispatch
accounts.gist: Bell's wife died Monday and was buried by friends; a mob organized Tuesday night took him from his home and hanged him to a tree, where his body was found the next morning.

accounts.label: Hamburg dispatch
accounts.gist: Col. J. M. Bell, 'a prominent citizen of this county', was hanged by a mob twenty miles south of Hamburg 'yesterday' after whipping his wife so severely on Christmas that she died.

accounts.label: Staunton Vindicator editorial
accounts.gist: On the night of the funeral 'the villagers and neighboring farmers' took the colonel out and hanged him, which the paper approved.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Shreveport or Pine Bluff text unchanged under crime headings such as 'Criminal Acts' or 'Crime Record', or in news digests.
Headlines such as 'A Merited Fate', 'A Brutal Wife-Murderer Lynched' and 'Brutal Husband Hanged' treated the accusation as proven and the hanging as deserved.
The Staunton Vindicator called it 'the best use that lynch law has been put to for a long time' and quoted a maxim against men who strike women.

conflicts.note: Bell appears in every version except the Chicago Tribune; the Dallas Herald's copy of the same Pine Bluff report reads Bell (A9), so 'Boll' is probably a typesetting or OCR variant.
The Hamburg dispatch puts the whipping on Christmas without saying when she died.
The Shreveport text says the body was found Wednesday morning, which may explain the Hamburg dispatch's 'yesterday'.
